label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
First time posting in one of these threads, so please bear with me. One of my blister-pack patients passed away recently, and her daughter came in to return the unused packs and her glucometer. I’ve been thinking about it since I got home.

Mrs. H was in her 80s and had been coming to us for almost seven years. Every week, same day, for her blister pack. She lived alone after her husband died. Walked with a cane. Every week she brought me something—poppy seed cake, usually, and once a jar of pickles I genuinely did not know what to do with. During Ramadan she remembered I was fasting and would wrap the cake in foil with my name on it and tell me not to eat it until sunset.

A couple of years ago a new prescription came through that interacted with her warfarin. I called the prescriber and we got it sorted. After that she told everyone I saved her life. I didn’t. I just did my job. But she was so proud of me.

Her daughter came in a couple of weeks ago with the unused blister packs and the glucometer. She also gave me a card. Inside, in Mrs. H’s handwriting, it said “for my Arabic daughter.” She’d written it a long time ago and never gave it to me.

I cried in the back room. My tech covered the counter for ten minutes and didn’t say anything, which was exactly what I needed.

School teaches us pharmacology, interactions, counselling points. Nobody teaches you how to say goodbye to a patient. Nobody teaches you what to say when their daughter puts a card in your hand. We’re not supposed to get attached, but you see someone every week for seven years. You learn their cane, their cake, their handwriting. I don’t know how you don’t get attached.

My father was a pharmacist in Egypt. He knew every family in the neighbourhood, and I used to think Canada would be different. It’s not. People still bring you pickles. People still remember you’re fasting. People still write your name on foil.

Anyway. I just wanted to put her somewhere. Does anyone else have a patient like this? The ones who become part of the rhythm of your week, and then one week they’re just not there?

reasons: The piece says the daughter came in 'a couple of weeks ago', but the request says she came on Nov 9, the same day the user is writing about, so the timing contradicts it.
